To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV-1 transactivator protein Tat induces dysfunction of tight junctions and Aβ-transferrin proteins in brain endothelial cells, and silencing the Cav- 1 gene plays a key role.
Cav-1 plays a key role against HIV-1-Tat-induced dysfunction of the BBB and Aβ accumulation in brain microvascular endothelial cells.
the silencing of the Cav-1 expression with shRNA plays an important role in the protection of HIV-1 Tat against the dysfunction of the blood brain barrier and Aβ-accumulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of HIV-1 Tat in blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and Aβ accumulation in the brain.
the mechanism of Aβ accumulation and the role of Cav-1, which may be useful in the prevention of HIV-1-induced dementia.
the role of Cav-1 shRNAs in the dysfunction of the blood brain barrier and amyloid β- (Aβ) transferring proteins induced by HIV-1 transactivator of transcription protein (Tat).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV-1 tat-induced downregulation in tight junctions and Aβ-transferrring proteins may result in the dysfunction of BBB and Aβ accumulation in the brain.
HIV-1 tat-induced downregulation and upregulation are mediated through the RhoA pathway.
the Cav-1 knock-down by RNA interference can protect the BBB against HIV-1-Tat-induced damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Cav-1 is a key regulator for the blood-brain-barrier integrity and Aβ accumulation in the brain.

the HIV-1 Tat protein is able to induce the dysfunction of tight junctions and Aβ-transfer proteins, which may result in the blood-brain-barrier dysfunction and Aβ accumulation in the brain, and the silencing of the Cav-1 with shRNA may be able to protect against HIV-1 induced blood-brain barrier dysfunction and Aβ deposition.

HIV-1 tat can induce the dysfunction of tight junctions and Aβ-transferrin proteins in brain endothelial cells, which may lead to the accumulation of A β in the brain and the development of AIDS dementia.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HIV-1 may induce the dysfunction of the blood brain barrier and Aβ deposition in the brain by downregulating the tight junction protein and Aβ-transferrin proteins, and Cav-1 may serve as a therapeutic target for HIV-1-induced neurotoxicity.
Cav-1 may play a role in regulating the function of the blood-brained barrier and Aβ transferring proteins.
Cav-1 may be a therapeutic target for the prevention of HIV-1 Tat-associated brain dysfunction.
